solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Cursed bedlamp’s alive, man held

indicators.note: alive in the sense of lively and stirring, so these letters are jumping about into a new order
something held is gripped from both sides, so one piece sits inside the other

blocks.note: taken as written, the possessive S included
a man is referred to as he

explanation.surface: Someone swears at a bedside lamp that has come alive and grabbed a man.
explanation.walkthrough: The bedlamp's letters are rearranged into BLASPMED, and HE is held in the middle to make BLASPHEMED.
explanation.definitionFit: To blaspheme is to swear profanely, so cursed and blasphemed are synonyms as past-tense verbs.

clue.text: Go wild and gamble it all away without bit of prudence

indicators.note: just a small bit of a word is wanted, namely its opening letter
without in its older sense of outside, so one piece wraps around the other

blocks.note: to lose the lot is to gamble away everything you have
the opening letter of prudence

explanation.surface: A warning against a reckless gambling spree that throws away all caution.
explanation.walkthrough: LOSE THE LOT is gambling everything away; slipping P inside the final word turns LOT into PLOT.
explanation.definitionFit: Losing the plot is an informal idiom for going crazy or losing self-control, the same as going wild.

clue.text: Light passion? That’s what row is about!

indicators.note: to be about something is to surround it, so one piece goes around the other

blocks.note: a set-to is a fight or argument
fire is ardour or strong passion

explanation.surface: A wry remark that couples quarrel because a gentle romance has sparked between them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Light passion' reads as a mild romance, but 'Light' is a verb, the definition. A set-to is a heated quarrel, split here around the passion.
explanation.definitionFit: To light something is to kindle it or make it burn, which is exactly what setting fire to it does.

clue.text: Hurt was a chart success around end of October

indicators.note: only the end of the word is wanted, its final letter
a phrase going around something encloses it, so one piece sits within the other

blocks.note: a record that charts well has had a hit
the closing letter of October

explanation.surface: A pop act was wounded even though it scored a hit single late in October.
explanation.walkthrough: The R slips into the first word of HAD HIT, after its second letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone badly affected by a blow or setback is described as hard-hit, a compound adjective meaning damaged or wounded.

clue.text: Music genre in which White Lines might sit?

definitions.text: Music genre in which White Lines might sit?

blocks.clueFragment: Music genre in which White Lines might sit?
blocks.note: surface reading: which style of music the hip-hop record White Lines belongs to
setter's reading: the painted white lines on a street, which run along its centre

explanation.walkthrough: White Lines is a 1983 hip-hop track by Grandmaster Flash and Melle Mel, so it is not easy-listening at all; the joke is that painted road markings sit right down the centre of the carriageway.
explanation.definitionFit: The genre label, often shortened to MOR, means bland easy-listening pop, and literally describes the centre of a street where markings go.

clue.text: Excessive yen to sit on short guys? That’s awful!

indicators.note: something short is cut down, so the last letter is lopped off
in a down entry, sitting on top means coming first, so the pieces stack in order

blocks.note: dear means overpriced, costing too much
Y is the symbol abbreviation for the Japanese yen
guys are men

explanation.surface: Someone complains about an overpriced yen for sitting on small men.
explanation.walkthrough: MEN loses its final letter to give ME. DEAR for 'expensive' is everyday British usage: a dear shop charges too much.
explanation.definitionFit: Deary me is a mild exclamation of dismay, the kind of thing said when hearing that something is awful.

clue.text: Fire assault rifle with live round

indicators.note: going round something means enclosing it, so one piece wraps the other

blocks.note: to be is to live or exist
AK is the designation of the Kalashnikov assault rifle, as in AK-47

explanation.surface: Firing a live round from an assault rifle on a shooting range.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fire', 'rifle' and 'round' all suggest gunfire, but 'round' is the container signal and 'Fire' means heating clay in a kiln.
explanation.definitionFit: Potters fire clay in a kiln, which means baking it hard with heat, so the two verbs are synonyms.

clue.text: One Billy Connolly might pick on at a gig?

definitions.text: One Billy Connolly might pick on at a gig?

blocks.clueFragment: One Billy Connolly might pick on at a gig?
blocks.note: surface reading: someone in the audience whom the comedian targets with insults during a show
setter's reading: an instrument plucked during a concert, which Connolly played in his folk days

explanation.walkthrough: Billy Connolly is a Scottish comedian known for heckling audiences, but he began as a folk musician; 'pick on' means play by plucking strings, not bully.
explanation.definitionFit: This stringed instrument is played by plucking or picking, and Connolly famously played one on stage.

clue.text: Island raising fine crops at its eastern tip

indicators.note: in a down entry, raising lifts the letters so they read bottom to top
east is the right-hand side, so the tip there is the final letter

blocks.note: OK means fine or all right
the last letter of crops

explanation.surface: A Greek island whose farming is concentrated on its eastern coast.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Raising fine crops' looks like farming, but 'raising' turns OK upside down and 'eastern tip' takes only the end of crops.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a Greek island in the Dodecanese, near the Turkish coast.

clue.text: One’s husband volunteers to meet Republican goddess

blocks.note: one is I, and the apostrophe-S is added
H is the abbreviation for husband
the TA, Territorial Army, is Britain's volunteer reserve force
R is the abbreviation for Republican

explanation.surface: A woman's husband signs up with volunteers to meet a Republican.
explanation.walkthrough: The Territorial Army is the British army's part-time volunteer reserve, hence TA.
explanation.definitionFit: Ishtar was the Mesopotamian deity of love, war and fertility, worshipped in Babylon and Assyria.

clue.text: Inability to hear case of defence? A fine point …

indicators.note: a case is the outer shell, so only the outside letters of the word are kept

blocks.note: the first and last letters of defence
taken as written
F is the pencil-grade abbreviation for fine
a ness is a headland or promontory, a point of land

explanation.surface: A courtroom remark: a defendant's inability to hear might be a fine point in their case.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition sits at the front and reads like a legal plea. NESS turns up in place names such as Loch Ness and Dungeness, the headland in Kent.
explanation.definitionFit: Deafness is the medical term for hearing loss, so it is a direct synonym of being unable to hear.

clue.text: … in upholding the employee’s originally overturned case

indicators.note: originally means at the origin, so each word gives only its opening letter
something overturned is flipped end to end, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: first letter of in
first letter of upholding
first letter of the
first letter of employee's

explanation.surface: Continuing the legal story: a fine point helped uphold an employee's case that had first been overturned.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis links the surface to 10 Across, but the wordplay stands alone. 'Case' looks like a lawsuit; it is the definition, a small container.
explanation.definitionFit: An etui is a small ornamental holder for needles or cosmetics, a crossword favourite for a little case.

clue.text: Woman pawns bloomers

blocks.note: Holly is a woman's name
to hock something is to pawn it

explanation.surface: A woman takes her underwear to the pawnshop.
explanation.walkthrough: Bloomers look like old-fashioned knickers, but here they are things that bloom.
explanation.definitionFit: Crosswords use bloomer for anything that flowers; these tall cottage-garden plants produce large showy blossoms on spikes.

clue.text: Beastly sort plastered in pink gunge

indicators.note: plastered means drunk, and a drunk staggers about, so the letters are scrambled

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A nasty character gets covered in pink slime, or a drunk lies in it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Beastly sort' reads as a horrible person, but it means a sort, or species, of beast. Gunge is British slang for sticky goo.
explanation.definitionFit: The king penguin is a species of large Antarctic bird, so it is one kind of animal, a beastly sort.

clue.text: Hewn tree in Glencoe with iodine on the stump?

definitions.note: a prepositional phrase defining a gerund: being on the stump is campaigning

indicators.note: hewn means chopped up, so the letters are cut and put back in another order

blocks.note: taken as written
I is the chemical symbol for iodine

explanation.surface: A tree felled in a Scottish glen, with iodine dabbed on what is left of the trunk.
explanation.walkthrough: Glencoe is a valley in the Scottish Highlands. The stump is not a tree stump: politicians once made speeches standing on one, hence 'on the stump' for campaigning.
explanation.definitionFit: Being on the stump is an idiom for touring and giving speeches during a campaign, which is canvassing for votes.

clue.text: In which cast hears Lear, perhaps

definitions.text: In which cast hears Lear, perhaps

indicators.note: to cast is to throw or mould anew, so these letters are thrown into another shape

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Actors run through King Lear together before opening night.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue does both jobs: 'cast' is the anagram signal and also the troupe of actors, and 'perhaps' flags King Lear as just one example of a play.
explanation.definitionFit: A practice run-through of a play, where a director listens to the actors deliver Shakespeare's tragedy before performance.

clue.text: Where products might be displayed in disarray

blocks.note: first meaning, taken literally: spread throughout a store
second meaning: the informal British phrase for scattered and chaotic

explanation.walkthrough: The first meaning is the literal one; the second is a British idiom for messy or disorganised.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means scattered everywhere in confusion, and literally describes goods placed throughout a retail store.

clue.text: Elizabethan old-timer bottles alcohol

indicators.note: to bottle is to hold something inside a container, so the letters are kept within the words

blocks.note: run across the end of the first word and the start of the next

explanation.surface: A Tudor-era veteran stores up his drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bottles' fits drink so well it reads as storing alcohol, but it signals the letters held inside 'Elizabethan old'.
explanation.definitionFit: Ethanol is the chemical name for the intoxicating ingredient found in beer, wine and spirits.

clue.text: Key-opened European desk okay to be put away?

indicators.note: a thing opened has something let into it, so one piece goes inside

blocks.note: E is the abbreviation for European
a desk is a kind of table
A is a musical key

explanation.surface: Asks whether a lockable European desk is fine to be stored.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put away' suggests tidying a desk, but it is slang for eating food; the question mark flags that sense. The key goes between the first two pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Food that is fit to be consumed is edible, and to put away food is informal for eating it.

clue.text: A tie is an accessory

blocks.note: first meaning: a bond or link of affection
second meaning: an extra fitting added to a tool or machine

explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a necktie as a fashion item; instead each half is a separate meaning of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both an emotional bond or connection and an add-on device fitted to equipment, like a vacuum nozzle.

clue.text: Promoters of commercial port to secure millions

indicators.note: to secure is to hold fast, so one piece is held inside the other

blocks.note: Aden is a seaport in Yemen
M is the abbreviation for millions

explanation.surface: Backers of a trading port try to bring in millions.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Commercial' is an adjective in the surface, describing the port, but it belongs to the definition, where it means an advert.
explanation.definitionFit: Advertising executives devise and sell television commercials, so they are people who promote them.

clue.text: Spots of corrosion finally found in service

indicators.note: finally points to the end, so only the last letter is used
something found in another sits inside it, so one piece is placed within

blocks.note: an ace is an unreturned serve in tennis
the final letter of corrosion

explanation.surface: Rust spots discovered at last during a car's service.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Service' suggests a garage, but it is a tennis serve; a serve the opponent cannot touch is an ace.
explanation.definitionFit: Acne is the skin condition that produces pimples, which are commonly called spots in Britain.

clue.text: Reddish-orange ruddy duck

blocks.note: both are mild British intensifiers, euphemisms for bloody
a duck is a score of nothing in cricket, so zero, O

explanation.surface: Describes a bird: a reddish duck, like the ruddy duck species.
explanation.walkthrough: The ruddy duck is a real bird, which sends the solver looking for waterfowl; instead ruddy is a polite curse and a duck is a cricket score of nought.
explanation.definitionFit: Flamingo names a pinkish-orange colour taken from the plumage of the wading bird.

clue.text: Cheek is a part of the face

blocks.note: first meaning: impudence or insolent talk
second meaning: one of the fleshy edges of the mouth

explanation.walkthrough: Cheek looks like the facial feature, which makes the second half seem to describe it; but it means backchat.
explanation.definitionFit: Giving someone lip means answering back rudely, and the word also names the fleshy rim around the mouth.

clue.text: Result of donning Wonderbra? Ding-dong!

blocks.note: first meaning, read literally: a push-up bra raises the chest
second meaning: British slang for a noisy quarrel

explanation.walkthrough: Wonderbra is a push-up bra brand. 'Ding-dong' sounds like a doorbell or a leery whistle, but in Britain a ding-dong is a heated row.
explanation.definitionFit: A bust-up is a loud argument or fight, the same as a ding-dong, and literally the chest lifted.

clue.text: Old writer yawning

blocks.note: O is the abbreviation for old
a pen is something you write with

explanation.surface: An elderly author is bored and stifling a yawn.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Yawning' suggests tiredness, but it means gaping wide, as in a yawning chasm.
explanation.definitionFit: A yawning gap or chasm is one that gapes wide, so the adjective describes something wide apart and uncovered.

clue.text: Needle girl repurposed as item of angling gear

indicators.note: something repurposed is remade for another use, so the letters are rebuilt in a fresh order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A sewing needle turned into a piece of fishing tackle, perhaps a hook.
explanation.walkthrough: A needle bent into a hook makes the surface plausible; the answer is not a hook but a fishing rig.
explanation.definitionFit: In coarse fishing, a weighted rig that holds bait still on the riverbed, used for bottom fishing with a sinker.
